title: CLAY COUNTY BOARD MEETS
full_story:
The Clay County Board met Tuesday night at the courthouse in Louisville and delved into a fairly lengthy discussion about Clay County Hospital.

Before that unfolded, Chairman Joe Goodman called the meeting to order and invited public comment.  Former member Ted Whitehead spoke briefly and invited members to attend the upcoming appreciation event put on by Snedeker Risk Management.  On top of handling the county’s insurance it also takes care of the administration of The Hope Trust, the health insurance option for Clay County employees.

After the meeting agenda was approved, Vice-Chairman Janice Brooks presented the Claims Committee Report.  It shows Paid Claims totaled $4,655,776 and Unpaid Claims of $79,382.  The board quickly approved the report.

Next, the board heard from representatives of the group SAFE Crisis Center in Effingham.  SAFE stands for Sexual Assault Family Emergencies.  Donna Rouleau and Traci Baucum explained how their organization helps children with a mission is to educate the community, provide advocacy for individuals and families, and offer empowerment to heal from sexual violence and other traumatic experiences.  The pair asked and Chairman Joe Goodman signed a proclamation making April Sexual Assault Awareness Month in Clay County.

Steve Lewis, Coordinator for Clay County ESDA (Emergency Services Disaster Agency)  addressed the board to discuss the county’s Hazard Mitigation Plan and to inform them about the county’s upcoming meeting.  On Wednesday, March 18 at 1:00pm at the Clay County Health Department.  The meeting is for members of entities that perform specific duties for residents, including when disaster strikes. Lewis says American Environmental of Springfield helps local governing bodies come up with disaster plans and offer instruction on how to apply for grant money that can aid their effort should the worst happen.  The meeting is also open to the public.

Clay County Hospital CEO/President Bob Sellers began his presentation by citing the excellent results from two inspections recently completed at the Clay County Hospital Pharmacy and the CCH Lab.  He then turned to the four items on the agenda.  First, was the renewal agreement with SSM Health.  The company began managing Clay County Hospital in 2013.  With the hospital seeing growth and increased revenue the agreement reduces the management fee from 3.4% to 3%, which will save over $100,000.  While the discussions continued for several minutes, in the end, the board approved the renewal unanimously.  The second item for the hospital was the disposition of the Burke House on the lake adjacent to CCH.  Sellers said they originally planned to tear the building down, but since it was a double-wide modular home and could be removed, they sought bids from area businesses.  Clay County State’s Attorney Phillip Givens stated that since it is owned by the county, bids must be sought via a legal notice.  Sellers then moved on to what is described as the HTCI Grant Project Executive Summary Budget Overrun.  This is the project that will see Shores Builders construct a new home for the Clay County Health Department on the CCH Campus, as well as make renovations to the hospital and the purchase of other hospital equipment.  The project’s original cost was $15 Million.  However, the approved plan was reexamined and was subject to changes ordered by the state and came in with a price tag of $18,5 Million, a cost overrun of $3.5 Million.  Sellers stated that they went back and made changes where they could to bring the cost back down.  When they finished, the final price was $17,835,834.  Sellers explained that the hospital has some cash reserves of $11 Million and the excess funds will be taken from that account.  This began a conversation about the possibility of using the reserve fund in other ways for the county.  It was pointed out that should something happen and financing is lost; the hospital would not survive very long.  After explanations from various members the discussion ended, and the measure was approved without dissent.  Before moving on, Sellers asked and members approved credentials for various healthcare professionals.

Lin Waller with the Clay County Health Department presented the Board of Health Report.  She stated that they are working at updating the food ordinance and nutrition guidelines but didn’t go into detail.  Waller also noted that March is National Colorectal Cancer Awareness Month.  She also spoke of the need for vaccinations, noting that on Monday, a young child in Effingham County died from Pertussis and another case of Measles has been reported in Illinois.   She encouraged parents to get their children immunized.

Sheriff Andy Myers presented his report and said that some of their communications equipment has failed and needs replaced.  The new equipment will cost $18,000 and said they need to get rolling on it.

In Executive Finance matters, Terry Hronec presented a resolution for the hospital to make a donation of $500,000 to Clay County’s Capital Expenditures Account.  The issue was put before the Hospital Committee; however, they couldn’t resolve the matter, and it was brought before the full board.  The money would be used solely for the purchase of equipment.  This discussion revived the topic of perhaps using the hospital reserves for other county needs or purchases.  When the vote was taken, the measure passed 9-4, with Troy Britton, Kelly Colclasure, Dave Johnson and Jeremy Kohn voting no.  Hronec also presented a request to purchase a warranty for their server in the amount of $3,020.  Members voted to approve the request unanimously.

Before the meeting adjourned, Clerk Amy Britton reminds everyone that the Primary Election is Tuesday, March 17.  She said there are 9,200 registered voters in Clay County and 160 people have voted early.  635 mail-in ballots were requested and 210 have been returned, meaning there are still 425 that have not arrived.  With all business complete, the meeting adjourned.

title: XENIA FIRE DEPARTMENT
full_story:
On Tuesday, at approximately 8:05 am, the Xenia Fire Department was dispatched to a report of a structure fire with possible entrapment in the rural 3000 block of Ironwood Road.

Upon arrival, units located a single-story residential structure with smoke visible inside the home.  An individual on scene advised responding personnel that a person was still trapped inside the residence.  Firefighters immediately initiated a primary search of the structure, followed by a secondary search.  Both searches confirmed that no occupants were inside the home.

Crews then began investigating the source of the smoke and found no further active fire.  The residence was ventilated using positive pressure fans to remove the remaining smoke from the structure.

Units responding to the scene included an engine, tanker, and brush truck, along with mutual aid assistance from the Flora Fire Department and Clay County Ambulance.

The cause of the fire remains under investigation by the Illinois State Fire Marshal’s Office in conjunction with the Clay County Sheriff’s Office and the Clay County State’s Attorney’s Office.

The reporting party, who was a nearby neighbor, was able to utilize a fire extinguisher to knock down the flames prior to the arrival of emergency personnel, helping to prevent further damage to the residence.

title: XENIA VILLAGE BOARD
full_story:
Following a call to order and a quick roll call Trustees turned their attention to the state of property in the village.  One derelict property in the area that was the focus of trustees turning to village attorney David Garavellia for recommendations on steps to move forward in dealing with the property and its absent owner.  Mr. Garawellia recommended GIS Mapping to locate information on the property owner and provide written citations along with copies of village ordinances for which the property owner is in violation.

In police business, Police Chief Jerry Burkett shared with trustees that everything was running smoothly.  Burkett had just put new tires on the police cruiser and completed Emergency Medical Response training at the Richland County Sheriff’s office.

Trustees approved the repair of a fire hydrant at Charley Brown Park with a 4-inch seal.  Trustees then discussed when the village would increase rates on water, sewer and garbage for the village with no action being taken at this time.

In Village Business trustees opted for a standard return to work policy.  Trustees also approved the continuance of the 1% grocery tax.  While a meeting with a representative for the IMRF state retirement fund is slated for some time in the summer.  Trustees also await an update on insurance claim made on the building at 601 Church Street and tabled a decision on approval on an ordinance to allow tiny homes in the village.

Trustees then approved a new debit card with a $1’000 limit to make large purchases.  Following previous discussions of improvements to be made to the school building.  No decision was made on the purchase of a tube heater for the cafeteria or on improvements to the gym floors.  However, at a previous board meeting approval was given for the purchase of new looks for the building doors in the amount of $600.  An estimate on an amount to repair or replace the roof is still pending.

The concession stand should be ready before the villages Ice cream social event where they will be raffling off a .22 hand gun.

title: CLAY COUNTY SHERIFF’S ACTIVITY REPORT
full_story:
Clay County Sheriff Andy Myers presented his monthly activity report during Tuesday’s Clay County Board meeting.  In the Report for February, the Sheriff’s Office issued a total of 23 Traffic Citations, made 17 Criminal Arrests and served 53 various Civil Papers.  A total of 21,563 miles were driven by Sheriff’s personnel during the month.

26 people were processed through the Clay County Jail during February.  There were 7 inmates in jail at the beginning of the month and 4 in jail at the end of the month.  The average daily jail population was 6.

Also, the Clay County Sheriff’s Office received a total of $2,598.18 during the month.  This includes:

The Sheriff’s Office handled approximately 481 complaints, 84 of which originated in Louisville and 64 in Clay City.  The Sheriff’s Office conducted 23 Criminal Investigations and 16 Accident Investigations during February.

title: BREAKFAST BITES AND BUSINESS
full_story:
The Flora Chamber of Commerce is sponsoring a Social Media Workshop titled Breakfast Bites and Business Insights on Wednesday, March 25th.

This session, presented in partnership with America’s SBDC Illinois and Illinois Eastern Community Colleges Business & Industry, will focus on how to effectively use social media to benefit and grow your business. Participants will enjoy light breakfast bites while gaining valuable insights from the featured speaker, Chris Forde, Program Director of Marketing and Communications for IECC.  Participants will learn practical tips, strategies, and tools to strengthen your online presence and better connect with your audience.

Whether you’re just getting started or looking to improve your current social media efforts, this workshop is designed to help your business shine online.  The workshop is free for Chamber Members and $5 for non members and will start at 8:30 am on Wednesday March 25th.  Space is limited RSVP today: https://forms.gle/Z46Cs5MCa1izi3ZYA

title: MASSAGE THERAPY CLINICALS
full_story:
Olney Central College’s Massage Therapy Program is accepting appointments for Spring clinicals.

The clinics are open to the public and will be held from 9:15 am to 2 pm on Saturday, March 20th, April 11th and April 24th at the West Richland Center in Noble.

The cost for a relaxing massage is $45 for an hour and $30 for half an hour.  A 20-minute chair massage is $20.

Clinics are by appointment only and can be made by calling 618-392-2430.  Callers should leave a message with their names, contact information and date desired.  Students will return phone messages during Monday and Wednesday evening classes to confirm appointments.

title: FAFSA NIGHT
full_story:
Olney Central College is hosting a FAFSA Completion Night from 3 to 6 pm on Tuesday, March 24th in Room 205 on the second floor of Dr. Kent L. Wattleworth Hall.

OCC Financial Aid experts will be available to answer questions and assist students and parents in Filing the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA).  Those attending should bring their FSA ID and 2024 tax returns to simplify the process.

While the event is open to everyone, the OCC Financial Aid staff especially encourages high school seniors who have not yet completed the FAFSA to attend, as it is required by the state for high school graduation.

For more information or if you have questions about the FAFSA, visit www.iecc.edu/financial, or contact OCC Financial Aid at 618-395-7777, ext. 2017.
